title: Cell Identity, Cell State and Disease

scenes.visual: Title card: Cell Identity, Cell State and Disease. Show a mixed tissue resolving into distinct identities, with variations within each identity.

scenes.tts: A tissue is not one average. Single-cell R N A sequencing reveals a mixture of cell types and changing states. A type is a stable identity, such as a T cell. A state is variation within it, such as cycling or stress. In melanoma, malignant cells within one tumour differed in cell-cycle programmes. That matters because separate clusters can represent different states of one type. A cluster needs an explanation before it gets a name.

scenes.visual: Resolve a tissue silhouette into different cell identities. Within one identity, show cycling and stressed states using symbols rather than new identity colours. Show malignant cells from one melanoma separating by cell-cycle programmes; retain the same malignant-identity colour. Label the groups as states, with provisional annotation tags.

scenes.tts: Separate the cells. Tag each cell's R N A with a shared barcode, then sequence and count. The matrix has genes as rows and cells as columns. Group similar cells, then annotate their clusters using known expression profiles.

scenes.visual: Show tissue dissociation, a shared barcode on each cell’s captured RNA, then a genes-by-cells count matrix. Group similar columns into clusters and compare with known profiles. Keep names provisional.

scenes.tts: But a cluster can also be an artifact. Two cells can share a barcode. Sample handling can separate cells that belong together. Check annotations with independent evidence. R N A does not measure protein. Cite seek measures surface proteins alongside R N A in the same cell.

scenes.visual: Show a doublet yielding a hybrid profile and different handling batches separating one identity. Place independent evidence beside provisional annotations. Show DNA-tagged antibodies measuring surface protein alongside RNA; label the method CITE-seq.

scenes.tts: An expression path suggests a transition. It does not track one living cell. Sequencing destroys each cell. Inherited barcodes establish ancestry by linking sisters and their descendants. In mouse blood progenitors, sisters shared fate biases their R N A profiles missed. Perturbation tests cause: block a candidate, check the outcome, then restore it.

scenes.visual: Label an expression trajectory as inferred pseudotime; show different sampled cells along it. Switch to a branching family with an inherited barcode: one sister is sequenced, the other produces labelled progeny. Show RNA similarity alongside differing future fates. Finish with candidate block, outcome check, and restoration as a general causal test.

scenes.tts: A bulk measurement can change because the mixture changes, even when expression within each type stays fixed. More cells expressing a gene strongly can raise the tissue average. Single-cell data separate those possibilities. But losing fragile cells during dissociation can bias the measured proportions.

scenes.visual: Compare two tissue mixtures. Increase the share of a high-expressing identity while keeping each identity’s per-cell expression fixed; the bulk signal rises. Show unchanged within-cluster expression beside changed proportions. Add fragile cells lost during dissociation as a sampling caution. Use no numerical labels.

scenes.tts: Tissue health also depends on balancing cell gain and loss. In mouse oesophagus, progenitors divide, daughters differentiate, and cells are shed. In crowded cultured sheets and zebrafish epidermis, living cells can be squeezed out. The extruded cells then die. Cell interactions help maintain that balance.

scenes.visual: Retain the epithelial-layer setting. Show basal progenitors dividing, differentiating daughters moving upward and shedding. Then show crowding-driven live-cell extrusion in MDCK sheets and zebrafish epidermis, followed by death outside the sheet. Label the systems so the extrusion result is not attributed to mouse oesophagus.

scenes.tts: A smaller point closes the story. In mouse oesophagus, Notch one mutant clones expanded without dividing faster. Tracking was consistent with more progenitor daughters and fewer differentiating ones.
